title: Which landmark is nearer?
hook: Pip and Juno use a number line to round. Sound stays off until you turn it on.
learning_intention: We are learning to choose the nearest multiple of ten or hundred using endpoints, distances and midpoints.
transcript:
Pip: Rounding means choosing a nearby landmark number, not changing how many you really have.
Juno: We round when an approximate value is useful — like about how many seats we need.
Pip: To round to the nearest ten, name the two neighbouring tens around your number.
Juno: For 224, the neighbours are 220 and 230. Count both distances.
Pip: 224 is 4 from 220 and 6 from 230, so it rounds to 220.
Juno: Your turn — which neighbouring tens surround 247?
Pip: A common mistake is picking the lower ten just because it looks smaller.
Juno: For 368, the distances are 8 and 2, so we round up to 370.
Pip: Predict: round 432 to the nearest ten.
Juno: At a midpoint like 450, both distances are 50. Neither is closer — we use the upward tie rule to choose 500.
Pip: New challenge: round 163 to the nearest ten using both distances.
Juno: Remember the intention — endpoints, distances, and the midpoint rule when the gaps are equal.

beats.text: Rounding means choosing a nearby landmark number. The real count stays the same.
We round when an approximate value is useful — not when someone needs an exact count.

scenes.title: Why landmarks and how to find them

beats.text: To round to the nearest ten, first name the two neighbouring tens around your number.
Neighbours are consecutive multiples of ten. Only one ten sits between them.

diagram.label: Find the neighbouring tens
diagram.srDescription: Number line from 220 to 230 with 224 marked between them and midpoint 225.

beats.text: Watch my thinking. 224 is 4 from 220 and 6 from 230.

diagram.label: 224 rounds to 220
diagram.srDescription: 224 is four units from 220 and six units from 230, so the nearer ten is 220.

beats.text: Four is the shorter distance, so 224 rounds to 220. The actual number remains 224.

feedback.correct: Yes — 240 and 250 are consecutive tens and 247 sits between them.
feedback.incorrect: Use consecutive multiples of ten with only one ten between them. 247 sits between 240 and 250.

beats.text: A common mistake is choosing the lower ten just because its value looks smaller.
For 368, compare distances: 8 to 360, and only 2 to 370.

diagram.label: 368 rounds to 370
diagram.srDescription: 368 is eight from 360 and two from 370, so it rounds to 370.

beats.text: The nearer landmark is 370. Compare gaps, not which endpoint looks smaller.
Use both distances before you choose.
beats.prompt: Round 432 to the nearest ten. 432 is 2 from 430 and 8 from 440.

diagram.label: Round 432
diagram.srDescription: 432 is two from 430 and eight from 440 on an equally spaced number line.

feedback.correct: Correct — the shorter distance is 2, so 432 rounds to 430.
feedback.incorrect: The shorter distance is 2 toward 430. Choose the endpoint with the smaller gap.

beats.text: For 450 to the nearest hundred, both distances are 50. Neither endpoint is closer.

diagram.label: Midpoint: equal distances
diagram.srDescription: 450 is exactly fifty from 400 and fifty from 500.

beats.prompt: Which reason correctly rounds 350 to the nearest hundred?
choices: Both distances are equal, so the upward tie rule selects 400.
The first digit always stays unchanged.

feedback.correct: Yes — equal distances create a tie, and our upward rule selects 400.
feedback.incorrect: At 350 both gaps are 50. Name the tie, then use the upward midpoint convention to choose 400.

beats.text: New number — not from the worked example. Round 163 to the nearest ten.

diagram.label: Your challenge: 163
diagram.srDescription: 163 lies between 160 and 170 on an equally spaced number line.

beats.prompt: 163 is 3 from 160 and 7 from 170. What is the nearest ten?

feedback.correct: Yes — distance 3 is shorter, so 163 rounds to 160.
feedback.incorrect: 3 is shorter than 7, so the nearer ten is 160. Keep 163 as the exact value.

beats.text: Remember: name the endpoints, compare both distances, and at an exact midpoint use the upward rule.
We are learning to choose the nearest multiple of ten or hundred using endpoints, distances and midpoints.
